src.q: Each tablet contains 100 mg of mebendazole.
Each tablet also contains 0.06 mg of sunset yellow (E110).

formulations.label: Oral suspension
formulations.note: Contains sucrose (500 mg/5 ml) and parahydroxybenzoates.

src.q: Each 5 ml of suspension contains 100 mg of mebendazole.
Each 5 ml also contains 500 mg of sucrose, 9 mg of methyl parahydroxybenzoate (E218) and 1 mg of propyl parahydroxybenzoate (E216).

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Gastrointestinal worm infections, single or mixed: threadworm/pinworm (Enterobius), whipworm (Trichuris), roundworm (Ascaris), hookworms (Ancylostoma, Necator). Not shown to work for cysticercosis.

src.q: For the treatment of Trichuris trichuria (whipworm), Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm or threadworm), Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Ancylostoma duodenale (common hookworm), Necator americanus (American hookworm) in single or mixed gastrointestinal infestations.
There is no evidence that Vermox Tablets are effective in the treatment of cysticercosis.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction (specialist-only, shared care or brand prescribing) in the UK tablet and suspension SmPCs checked.

items.t: Threadworm (enterobiasis): 100 mg (one tablet or 5 ml) as a single dose; a second dose after 2 weeks is highly recommended if re-infection is suspected.

src.q: For the control of enterobiasis a single tablet is administered. It is highly recommended that a second tablet is taken after two weeks, if re-infection is suspected.
Enterobiasis: 1 x 5 ml (1 dosing cup).

items.t: Whipworm, roundworm, hookworm and mixed infections: 100 mg (one tablet or 5 ml) twice daily for 3 days.

src.q: For the control of trichuriasis, ascariasis and hookworm infections, one tablet twice a day for three consecutive days.
Ascariasis, trichuriasis, ancylostomiasis, necatoriasis and mixed infections: 1 x 5 ml (1 dosing cup) bd for three days.

items.t: Over 2 years: adult dose. Under 2 years: not recommended (section 4.4); not well studied and no dose recommendation can be made. Children 1 to 2 years: use only if the potential benefit justifies the risk and the worms significantly affect nutrition or development. Under 1 year: should not be used. Convulsions have been reported very rarely in children, including infants under 1 year.

src.q: Not recommended in the treatment of children under 2 years
Because of the lack of sufficient safety data, Vermox should not be used in children below the age of 1 year
Therefore, Vermox should be used in children aged 1-2 years only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
Convulsions in children, including in infants below 1 year of age, have been reported very rarely during post-marketing experience

items.t: Young children who cannot swallow tablets: consider the suspension. Tablets can be crushed for a young child; always supervise.

src.q: Crush the tablet before giving it to a young child. Always supervise a child while they are taking this medicine.

items.t: Pregnancy; hypersensitivity to mebendazole or any component.

src.q: Vermox is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients who have shown hypersensitivity to the product or any components.

items.t: Metronidazole: avoid using together (a possible link with Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN in one outbreak).

src.q: Although there are no additional data on this potential interaction, concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided.

items.t: Rare reversible liver function disturbances, hepatitis and neutropenia at usual doses; agranulocytosis and glomerulonephritis in high-dose echinococcosis treatment.

src.q: There have been rare reports of reversible liver function disturbances, hepatitis and neutropenia described in patients who were treated with mebendazole at recommended dosages for indicated conditions

items.t: Children under 2 years: not recommended (see paediatric).

src.q: Not recommended in the treatment of children under 2 years

items.t: Suspension: contains sucrose; hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Impaired liver function, metabolism or biliary elimination may raise mebendazole levels.

src.q: Impaired hepatic function, impaired metabolism, or impaired biliary elimination may lead to higher plasma levels of mebendazole.

items.t: Metronidazole: avoid the combination (possible Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN).

src.q: Concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided (see section 4.4).

items.t: Cimetidine may inhibit mebendazole metabolism and raise its levels.

src.q: Concomitant treatment with cimetidine may inhibit the metabolism of mebendazole in the liver, resulting in increased plasma concentrations of the drug.

renal.note: The UK tablet and suspension SmPCs give no renal dosing advice.

items.t: No dose advice. Mainly metabolised by the liver; impaired hepatic function or biliary elimination may raise mebendazole levels. Rare reversible liver function disturbances and hepatitis reported.

src.q: Impaired hepatic function, impaired metabolism, or impaired biliary elimination may lead to higher plasma levels of mebendazole.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated in pregnancy; anyone who is or may be pregnant should not take it (animal studies showed developmental harm).

src.q: Since Vermox is contraindicated in pregnancy, patients who think they are, or may be, pregnant should not take this preparation.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): threadworms do not harm the baby. Strict hygiene measures may clear them; if not, or if medicine is preferred, mebendazole can be used: no evidence of harm and little is absorbed. Some may prefer hygiene measures first and delay mebendazole until after about 12 weeks.

src.q: If hygiene measures do not clear up threadworms, or medicine use is preferred, mebendazole (Vermox®, Ovex®) can be used.
There is no evidence that mebendazole harms the baby, and it is only absorbed into the body in small amounts.
some women may prefer to try hygiene measures first and delay mebendazole treatment until the baby is fully developed at around 12 weeks of pregnancy

items.t: A small amount passes into breast milk: use with caution.

src.q: Therefore, caution should be exercised when Vermox is administered to breast-feeding women.

items.t: No effect on fetuses and offspring when given to male and female rats before conception. BUMPS: no increased risk expected if the father used mebendazole around conception.

src.q: had no effect upon fetuses and offspring
We would not expect any increased risk to your baby if the father had threadworms or used mebendazole before or around the time your baby was conceived.

items.t: Common: abdominal pain. Uncommon: abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea, vomiting.

src.q: Gastrointestinal Disorders Abdominal paina Abdominal discomforta; Diarrhoeaa; Flatulencea Nauseaa, Vomitinga

items.t: Rare: hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis, convulsions, hepatitis, neutropenia/agranulocytosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, angioedema, glomerulonephritis.

src.q: Hypersensitivity including anaphylactic reaction and anaphylactoid reactionb
Toxic epidermal necrolysisb; Stevens-Johnson syndromeb

monitoring.note: The UK tablet and suspension SmPCs give no routine monitoring advice for standard short courses.

items.t: Tablets may be chewed or swallowed whole; crush for a young child and supervise. Suspension: use the 5 ml dosing cup; consider it for young children who cannot swallow tablets.

src.q: Tablets may be chewed or swallowed whole.
Vermox oral suspension should be considered for patients such as young children who are unable to swallow the tablet.

items.t: Threadworm: take a second dose after 2 weeks if re-infection is suspected.

src.q: It is highly recommended that a second tablet is taken after two weeks, if re-infection is suspected.

items.t: Do not take if you are or may be pregnant (SmPC).

src.q: patients who think they are, or may be, pregnant should not take this preparation

rules.action: SmPC: do not use in pregnancy or possible pregnancy. BUMPS view differs (see next rule).

rules.consequence: No evidence that mebendazole harms the baby; little is absorbed.
rules.action: BUMPS: try strict hygiene measures first if preferred; mebendazole can be used if they fail; some may delay it until after about 12 weeks.

src.q: If hygiene measures do not clear up threadworms, or medicine use is preferred, mebendazole (Vermox®, Ovex®) can be used.
There is no evidence that mebendazole harms the baby, and it is only absorbed into the body in small amounts.

rules.consequence: A small amount passes into breast milk.

src.q: Limited data from case reports demonstrate that a small amount of mebendazole is present in human milk following oral administration.
Therefore, caution should be exercised when Vermox is administered to breast-feeding women.

rules.consequence: Insufficient safety data; convulsions reported very rarely.

src.q: Because of the lack of sufficient safety data, Vermox should not be used in children below the age of 1 year

rules.consequence: Not extensively studied under 2 years; no dose recommendation can be made; convulsions reported very rarely.
rules.action: Not recommended under 2 years. If used at 1 to 2 years: only if the potential benefit justifies the risk, and only when the worms significantly affect nutrition or physical development.
rules.sourceWording: Not recommended in the treatment of children under 2 years

src.q: Not recommended in the treatment of children under 2 years
Therefore, Vermox should be used in children aged 1-2 years only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
Vermox should only be given to very young children if their worm infestation interferes significantly with their nutritional status and physical development.

rules.consequence: Possible association with Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (case-control study of one outbreak).
rules.sourceWording: concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided

src.q: A case-control study of a single outbreak of Stevens-Johnson syndrome /toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) suggested a possible association with the concomitant use of metronidazole with mebendazole.
Concomitant use of mebendazole and metronidazole should be avoided (see section 4.4).
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.
